\label{ch:es-desde-entonces}

\begin{chapteropening}

\section[desde entonces]{desde entonces — since then}

\label{lesson:ES-C537-desde-entonces}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for as soon as, then the Spanish for the moment that.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: desde entonces}
\textbf{desde entonces} — \textquotedblleft{}since then\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Desde entonces no lo he visto.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{I haven't seen him since then.}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{desde entonces} is built on \emph{desde} 'since' and \emph{entonces}, which comes from Latin \emph{in tunc} 'at that time' (EtymDB), with an \emph{-s} added on the end.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{desde entonces}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{desde entonces}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{desde entonces}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for as soon as, then the Spanish for the moment that, then say \emph{desde entonces} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does desde entonces mean? (\textquotedblleft{}Since then\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[hasta entonces]{hasta entonces — until then}

\label{lesson:ES-C537-hasta-entonces}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for the moment that, then the Spanish for since then.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: hasta entonces}
\textbf{hasta entonces} — \textquotedblleft{}until then\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Hasta entonces, nadie sabía nada.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{Until then, nobody knew anything.}
\end{quote}

In a goodbye: \emph{¡Hasta entonces!} — see you then!

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{hasta entonces} is built on \emph{hasta}, which is usually traced to Arabic \emph{ḥattā} 'until', and \emph{entonces}, from Latin \emph{in tunc} 'at that time' (EtymDB).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{hasta entonces}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{hasta entonces}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{hasta entonces}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for the moment that, then the Spanish for since then, then say \emph{hasta entonces} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does hasta entonces mean? (\textquotedblleft{}Until then\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[al día siguiente]{al día siguiente — the next day, the following day}

\label{lesson:ES-C537-al-dia-siguiente}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for since then, then the Spanish for until then.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: al día siguiente}
\textbf{al día siguiente} — \textquotedblleft{}the next day, the following day\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Al día siguiente volvió a la tienda.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The next day he went back to the shop.}
\end{quote}

In a story about the past use \emph{al día siguiente}, not \emph{mañana}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{al día siguiente} is built on \emph{siguiente} 'following', from \emph{seguir}, which comes from Latin \emph{sequī} 'to follow' (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{al día siguiente}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{al día siguiente}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{al día siguiente}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for since then, then the Spanish for until then, then say \emph{al día siguiente} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does al día siguiente mean? (\textquotedblleft{}The next day, the following day\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[hace poco]{hace poco — a short time ago, recently}

\label{lesson:ES-C537-hace-poco}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for until then, then the Spanish for the next day.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: hace poco}
\textbf{hace poco} — \textquotedblleft{}a short time ago, recently\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Hace poco me mudé a esta ciudad.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{I moved to this city a short time ago.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Hace} + time = ago: \emph{hace dos años}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{hace poco} is built on \emph{hace}, from \emph{hacer}, inherited from Latin \emph{facere} 'to make', and \emph{poco}, from Latin \emph{paucus} 'few, little' (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{hace poco}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{hace poco}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{hace poco}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for until then, then the Spanish for the next day, then say \emph{hace poco} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does hace poco mean? (\textquotedblleft{}A short time ago, recently\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[anteayer]{anteayer — the day before yesterday}

\label{lesson:ES-C537-anteayer}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for the next day, then the Spanish for a short time ago.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: anteayer}
\textbf{anteayer} — \textquotedblleft{}the day before yesterday\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Anteayer hubo un accidente en mi calle.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The day before yesterday there was an accident on my street.}
\end{quote}

In Latin America people also say \emph{antier}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{anteayer} is built on \emph{ante} 'before' and \emph{ayer} 'yesterday', which comes from Latin \emph{herī} 'yesterday' (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{anteayer}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{anteayer}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{anteayer}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for the next day, then the Spanish for a short time ago, then say \emph{anteayer} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does anteayer mean? (\textquotedblleft{}The day before yesterday\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
